# Code review iteration

Reviewed the whole `octolab/config` module at commit `d8771f2 2022-03-26`: all Go
sources (`feature.go`, `secret.go`, `http/server.go`), their tests, `go.mod`/`go.sum`,
`tools/`, both GitHub Actions workflows, `.golangci.yml`, the Makefile/Taskfile/bin
scaffolding, and README/docs. The angle is a return-to-maintenance assessment against
the 2026 Go ecosystem (Go 1.26 era): real defects and API traps first, then
idiomaticity, with all repo-wide staleness consolidated into a single migration
finding. No previous review files exist in `.github/reviews/`, so every finding below
is new. `.github/issues/` and `.github/roadmap/` were ignored as offline backlog dumps.

Severity: **Crit** / **High** / **Med** / **Low** / **Nit**.
Class: `correctness` · `security` · `concurrency` · `perf` · `api` · `idiom` · `modern` · `test` · `build` · `docs`.

## 1. Continuous integration is dead and the toolchain baseline is four years stale

Anchor: .github/workflows/ci.yml:33 (plus tools.yml:18, go.mod:3, .golangci.yml:10, tools/go.mod:167).

```yaml
runs-on: ubuntu-18.04
```

Nothing in this repository's automation can run today. Consolidated inventory:

- **CI runners are gone.** `ubuntu-18.04` was removed from GitHub Actions in April
  2023 (`ci.yml:33,58,79`, `tools.yml:18,42`). Every job fails at scheduling, so the
  repo has effectively had no CI for three years.
- **Actions are deprecated or shut down.** `actions/checkout@v2` and
  `actions/cache@v2` run on retired Node runtimes; `actions/upload-artifact@v3` /
  `download-artifact@v3` (`ci.yml:50,63`) were hard-disabled by GitHub on
  2025-01-30; `paambaati/codeclimate-action@v2.7.5` targets Code Climate Quality,
  which has been sunset in favor of Qlty. The workflows also lack a `permissions:`
  block, so they run with the legacy permissive `GITHUB_TOKEN`.
- **Go version matrix is archaeology.** Testing 1.11–1.18 (`ci.yml:22-31`,
  `Makefile:5`) is pointless; only the last two minors are supported. `go 1.11` in
  `go.mod:3` blocks every post-2018 language feature and makes `govulncheck` and
  modern analyzers less effective.
- **Dependencies are archived.** `gopkg.in/yaml.v2` (go.mod:7) — the whole go-yaml
  project was archived in April 2025; it is a test-only dependency but still lands
  in the module graph of every consumer. `testify v1.7.1` is many releases behind.
- **Lint stack no longer exists in this form.** golangci-lint v1.45.2
  (`tools/go.mod:7`) predates the v2 config format; `.golangci.yml` enables linters
  that were deprecated in v1.49 and removed since (`deadcode`, `structcheck`,
  `varcheck`, `golint`), plus `exportloopref`/`looppointer`, obsolete after Go 1.22
  changed loop-variable semantics. The `fetch:` key (`.golangci.yml:3`) is not a
  valid config key and fails `golangci-lint config verify` in v2.
- **tools/ pattern is superseded.** The blank-import `tools.go` +
  `replace`-to-personal-forks (`tools/go.mod:167-168`,
  `github.com/kamilsk/golangci-lint`, `kamilsk/go-tools`) is exactly what the
  `tool` directive in go.mod (Go 1.24+) replaced; the forks themselves are frozen
  at 2022 versions.
- **Missing today's table stakes:** no `dependabot.yml`/Renovate config in-repo, no
  `govulncheck` step, no CodeQL/OpenSSF scorecard, no `GOTOOLCHAIN` policy.

**Fix.** One modernization pass: bump `go.mod` to `go 1.25` (or current-1), run
`go mod tidy && go fix ./...`; drop yaml.v2 for `goccy/go-yaml` in tests or test the
marshaler contract without a YAML dependency; rewrite both workflows on
`ubuntu-latest` with `actions/checkout@v4`+`actions/setup-go@v5` (built-in module
cache), a two-version Go matrix, `permissions: {contents: read}`, and a
`govulncheck` job; replace Code Climate with native coverage summary or Codecov;
delete `tools/` in favor of `go get -tool golangci-lint@v2` and run
`golangci-lint migrate` on the config; add `dependabot.yml` for gomod + actions.

## 2. Find methods cannot distinguish a missing feature from a disabled one

Anchor: feature.go:40-47 and feature.go:51-58.

```go
func (features Features) FindByID(id [16]byte) Feature {
	for _, feature := range features {
		if feature.ID == id {
			return feature
		}
	}
	return Feature{}
}
```

Both finders return the zero `Feature` on a miss. For a feature-flag type this is an
API trap: `features.FindByName("new-checkout").Enabled` yields `false` both when the
flag is configured off and when the name is a typo that matches nothing. Callers
cannot detect misconfiguration, and the zero value is a legitimate-looking `Feature`
with empty ID and name that can propagate far from the call site. The doc comment
documents the behavior, but documentation does not make a sentinel-zero-value lookup
idiomatic — Go's own idiom for this is the comma-ok pair (`v, ok := m[k]`).

**Fix.** Return `(Feature, bool)` from both finders (the README already declares the
module is not BC-safe across majors, so an API break is on the table). If the break
is unwanted now, add `LookupByID`/`LookupByName` with comma-ok semantics and
deprecate the current pair.

## 3. Duration fields promise JSON support they cannot deliver

Anchor: http/server.go:8-11.

```go
ReadTimeout       time.Duration `json:"read-timeout"        yaml:"read-timeout"`
```

`time.Duration` is an `int64`, and `encoding/json` has no special handling for it:
unmarshaling `{"read-timeout": "5s"}` fails with a type error, and the only accepted
input is a raw nanosecond count (`5000000000`), which nobody writes in a config file
by hand. Marshaling likewise emits nanosecond integers. Meanwhile the YAML path
behaves differently: yaml.v2/v3 special-case `time.Duration` and parse `"5s"` via
`time.ParseDuration`. So the same struct accepts human-readable durations in YAML
but rejects them in JSON — a silent asymmetry in the flagship struct of a
configuration toolkit. (Go still has no stdlib fix for this; `encoding/json/v2`
keeps durations as a known pain point requiring custom options.)

**Fix.** Introduce a `Duration` wrapper type in this package implementing
`json.Marshaler`/`json.Unmarshaler` (and `encoding.TextMarshaler`/`TextUnmarshaler`,
which also covers TOML and yaml.v3) that accepts both `"5s"` strings and integer
nanoseconds, and use it for the four timeout fields. Alternatively drop the `json`
tags and document the struct as YAML-only; the current state is the worst of both.

## 4. Package http shadows the standard library net-http

Anchor: http/server.go:1.

```go
package http
```

Any consumer wiring this config into a real server imports both this package and
`net/http` in the same file — which is essentially the only use case for a type
called `Server` holding `ReadTimeout`/`MaxHeaderBytes`. That forces an alias
(`confighttp "go.octolab.org/toolkit/config/http"`) at every call site. Shadowing
stdlib package names is explicitly discouraged by Go style guidance today
(staticcheck, Google Go style guide) because it degrades readability exactly where
the package is used most.

**Fix.** Rename the package (e.g. `httpconfig`, or fold the struct into the root
`config` package as `config.HTTPServer`). Major-version-break rules from the README
apply. While touching it, add the natural missing method — a helper that produces a
configured `*net/http.Server` (`func (s Server) Build() *http.Server`) — so the
struct does something beyond holding tags.

## 5. Secret has no reveal accessor and silently destroys data on round-trip

Anchor: secret.go:4-29.

```go
type Secret string

func (Secret) String() string { return "***" }
```

The masking coverage is actually good — `fmt` resolves `Stringer`/`GoStringer` for
`%v`, `%+v`, `%#v`, `%s`, `%q`, `%x`, and the marshalers cover JSON, XML/text, and
YAML. Three real problems remain:

1. **No sanctioned way to read the value.** The only escape hatch is a raw
   `string(secret)` conversion. That is invisible to grep/code review (it looks like
   any other conversion), unauditable, and encourages ad-hoc casts scattered through
   consumer code. Every serious secret type (e.g. modern `redact`-style packages)
   pairs masking with an explicit, greppable accessor.
2. **Round-trip destruction.** `MarshalJSON`/`MarshalText`/`MarshalYAML` return
   `***` unconditionally, so any consumer that persists its config back to disk
   (a common pattern: load, mutate, save) silently overwrites real credentials with
   `***`. The doc comment says "while printing", but marshalers are serialization,
   not printing; the failure is data loss, not just cosmetics.
3. **Undocumented leak vectors.** `encoding/gob` and other binary codecs that ignore
   `TextMarshaler` serialize the raw value, as does string concatenation and use as
   a map key in formatted output. The type's contract should state what it does and
   does not protect against; today the one-line comment overpromises.

**Fix.** Add `func (s Secret) Reveal() string { return string(s) }` (name it
`Expose`/`Value` to taste) and document it as the single sanctioned access point.
Document the marshaling behavior as intentionally lossy and enumerate the known
bypasses (gob, direct conversion). Consider implementing `slog.LogValuer`
(`return slog.StringValue("***")`) now that `log/slog` is the standard logging API.

## 6. Feature ID is a raw 16-byte array instead of a UUID type

Anchor: feature.go:10.

```go
ID      [16]byte
```

The field is transparently a UUID, but exposing it as an anonymous `[16]byte` pushes
all construction, parsing, and formatting onto every caller: no way to build one
from `"a1b2..."` without hand-rolling hex decoding, `String()` output ignores the ID
entirely, and `FindByID` (feature.go:40) forces callers to produce a byte array to
look anything up. In 2026 the ecosystem-standard is `github.com/google/uuid.UUID`
(itself a `[16]byte`, so the representation is compatible), or at minimum a named
`type ID [16]byte` with `Parse`/`String`.

**Fix.** Either adopt `uuid.UUID` for the field and `FindByID` parameter (one small,
ubiquitous dependency), or define `type ID [16]byte` in this package with
`ParseID(string) (ID, error)` and `String()`. Both keep struct layout identical.

## 7. Server config has zero test coverage and Secret tests miss leak vectors

Anchor: http/server.go:6-13; secret_test.go:23-53; feature_test.go:47-72.

The `http` package has no test file at all. Its only behavior is its struct tags —
and precisely that untested behavior hides the JSON/YAML duration asymmetry of
finding 3: a simple round-trip test (`yaml.Unmarshal` and `json.Unmarshal` of
`read-timeout: 5s`) would have exposed it years ago. The `Secret` test matrix covers
`%#v`, `%s`, JSON, XML, YAML but not `%q`/`%x`/`%v` (cheap to add and they pin the
`fmt` contract), not gob (would document a known bypass), and no unmarshal direction
at all — nothing asserts what happens when `***`-masked output is read back
(finding 5). `Features.FindByID`/`FindByName` tests never exercise the miss-on-
lookalike case (a zero-ID feature present in the list), which is exactly the
ambiguity of finding 2.

**Fix.** Add `http/server_test.go` with JSON+YAML round-trip cases for all fields
(these become the executable spec for whatever fix 3 lands on); extend the Secret
matrix with `%q`, `%x`, `%v`, and a gob case documenting expected leakage; add a
zero-value-collision case for the finders.

## 8. README and docs are still template placeholders

Anchor: README.md:14,20,24; docs/readme.mdx:1; docs/package.json:4.

The Idea, Motivation, and How-to sections of the README each contain a literal
`...`. The "full description" link points to a Notion page — content invisible to
pkg.go.dev and search, and hostage to a personal workspace. `docs/readme.mdx` is a
single heading; `docs/package.json` still carries the metadata of the
`octomation/go-module` template (homepage, repository, bugs all point at the
template repo, `"test": "exit 1"`), and its MDX 2.x dependency tree is itself stale.
For a public library, the README is the product page; six badges above three empty
sections reads worse than no README.

**Fix.** Write the three sections (a package this small needs ~15 lines: Secret
masking, feature flags, HTTP server config, one usage snippet each); move the
essential design rationale from Notion into the repo; either delete `docs/` or make
it real — half-initialized template machinery is pure maintenance surface.

## 9. Era-bound idioms: empty interface, named returns, dot imports

Anchor: secret.go:22, secret.go:17, feature_test.go:8, secret_test.go:13.

Small signs of the codebase's 2019–2022 vintage: `MarshalYAML() (interface{}, error)`
should be `any` since Go 1.18; `MarshalText() (text []byte, err error)` declares
named returns it never uses (secret.go:17) — plain `([]byte, error)` matches the
other marshalers; both test files dot-import the package under test
(`. "go.octolab.org/toolkit/config"`), which staticcheck flags as ST1001 and current
style guides reject even in external test packages; `Feature.String` could use
`strconv.FormatBool` instead of a `fmt.Sprintf("%v")` round-trip. None of these are
defects; together they signal the module predates modern gofmt/staticcheck defaults
and will produce warnings the moment the lint stack from finding 1 is revived.

**Fix.** Mechanical pass after the toolchain bump: `gofmt` rewrites `interface{}` →
`any` (`gofmt -r 'interface{} -> any'`), drop the named returns, replace dot imports
with a named import, and let the refreshed golangci-lint config keep it that way.
